vignette:
She first begins talking about the night her world changed by saying she had spent it, as she often did, at her drafting table, one eye on the blueprints spread across the desk and the other on her phone, waiting for a message from her adult son. He is driving home late from work when the call comes from the hospital. She remembers the strange, flat voice on the line, the way the words do not seem to belong to her life: collision, serious injuries, come now. In the car on the way there, she grips the steering wheel so hard her hands ache, and by the time she reaches the emergency department she feels as though she has already left her body somewhere behind her.

Her son survives, but the injuries are severe and the recovery is long. She spends the first weeks moving between hospital rooms, specialists, and waiting areas, learning to read medical updates the way she once read site plans. Before the accident, she had been the person others relied on for calm problem-solving; she is used to managing budgets, deadlines, and difficult clients. In the hospital, that same competence turns inward and becomes a way to survive. She starts keeping meticulous notes, writing down medications, appointments, names of nurses, questions for doctors. If she cannot control the outcome, she tells herself, she can at least control the details.

But the details do not stay orderly. She begins to wake each morning already braced for bad news. Her mind returns to the crash in fragments she never witnessed directly but reconstructs repeatedly from police reports, photographs, and her son's halting account. She imagines the impact again and again, the sound of metal, the sudden violence of it, and she hates how vivid the images become when she is alone. At work she can still produce elegant designs, but now she has to reread the same line several times because her concentration slips. She finds herself staring at a façade drawing without taking it in, then realizing minutes have passed. Once reliable and composed, she now feels brittle, as if one more demand might break her.

The accident changes the way she moves through the world. Driving becomes difficult first on the route to the hospital and later anywhere on roads like the one where the collision happened. She avoids intersections that remind her of the night, and she takes longer paths even when they make no sense. When a siren passes, her chest tightens and she feels instantly alert, scanning for danger before she has fully registered where she is. Sleep is no longer restful. She falls asleep exhausted, only to wake in the early hours with her heart pounding, mind already racing ahead to images of her son in pain. Some nights she checks her phone repeatedly, needing to make sure he has not tried to call while she was asleep. Other nights she gives up on sleep entirely and sits in the dark kitchen with a cup of tea growing cold in her hands.

She does not speak much about how frightened she is, even with people who care about her. Since her divorce, she has learned to keep painful things contained, and this is one more thing she feels she must hold together for everyone else. Her son needs her to be steady. Her colleagues expect her to be available. Friends tell her he is lucky to be alive, and she nods, but what she feels most often is not gratitude. It is terror, anger, and a heavy guilt that she cannot name easily. She wonders if she should have called him earlier that night, if she should have insisted he rest, if there was any way she might have prevented the accident. These thoughts come relentlessly, with the same sharp logic she uses at work, though here they offer no resolution.

Months later, her son has physically improved, but she remains stuck in a state of alarm. She is still the architect she has always been-precise, observant, capable of seeing structure where others see only mess-but now she also lives with a persistent sense that catastrophe is never far away. She goes through her days managing it quietly, functioning on the outside while carrying the crash with her in the background, always listening for the next sudden call that might split her life open again.
